title: Chicago pianists: Joe Sullivan, Stacy and Grunewald
summary: They discuss why Chicago white pianists were weak, Joe Sullivan's emergence, Jess Stacy, and Grunewald's arranging at WGN.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well, how did Joe Sullivan come up? Out of nowhere?
I can't tell you that, because I don't know. I've known him ever since, but I don't know.
There are several pianists around Chicago. And you're right. None of them were remarkable, except Joe.

Joe hit the first water. And the rest of them came from outside. People like Stacy, for example, was not a native. No. Chicago. I don't know how long he lived in Chicago, but he started out in Russia.
Yes. Well, I certainly don't associate art with the early days at all. No. He didn't.
Well, he showed up by 1928, but that isn't the 24 that you're talking about.

And I can't remember when I first ran into jazz. He was sort of a legend to me for quite a long time. Art Grunewald, on the other hand, I don't want to not pay proper attention to him. He really was good. Probably still is.

He's capable, and yet there isn't the strong jazz elements, which came just a few years later. Art plays a nice steady piano, and if he weren't playing with a jazz band, you might not identify it as great jazz music.
I suppose not. But he's capable enough with a jazz band.
Supply the beat, and he rides along very nicely on it.
He also liked the Lower Indiana stuff, associated with it, because he's the only person I've ever known who could play that Boneyard Shuffle.

And he made arrangements. When he was working with the Gold Cat Orchestra at WGN, he would arrange mix tunes for them. He took delight in that. He arranged the Wolverine's Limehouse, which they recorded. However, that was a different Wolverine's. It was Voino's band, but a band that apparently didn't contain any of the early men. And so he was quite understanding, at any rate, and rather sophisticated for a Dixie former. Here again we come to that question, whether without New Orleans there might have been a high order of art in the dance music around Chicago. We now think that it's quite artful, because there are many conscious efforts to draw progress and draw high virtuosity out of the men, and develop the most out of the music. In your opinion, they did not, in those years, acknowledge that New Orleans was the only influence.
